bullet_groups.bullet: Designed the order book with std::list FIFOs per price level in a std::map and an order-ID hash map to make cancels O(1), which ran the full replay at 1.26M events/sec and hit a 1.2 µs p99 on a separate 2M-event run

feedback.bullet: Designed the order book with std::list FIFOs per price level in a std::map and an order-ID hash map to make cancels O(1), which ran the full replay at 1.26M events/sec and hit a 1.2 µs p99 on a separate 2M-event run
feedback.problem: The first half is a stack of four C++ type names ('std::list FIFOs per price level in a std::map and an order-ID hash map') before the reader learns the goal ('make cancels O(1)'). The numbers at the end are strong but come after the hardest part to read.
feedback.why_it_matters: A recruiter's eye stalls on the type names and may miss 1.26M events/sec, which is the number an HFT screener is looking for. An engineer will understand it either way.
feedback.suggested_direction: Put the purpose (instant cancels, orders kept in arrival order at each price) before the data-structure names, or name the structures in plain terms ('a queue per price level, plus a lookup by order ID').

feedback.bullet: Designed the order book with std::list FIFOs per price level in a std::map and an order-ID hash map to make cancels O(1), which ran the full replay at 1.26M events/sec and hit a 1.2 µs p99 on a separate 2M-event run
feedback.problem: The opening is a noun stack ('std::list FIFOs per price level in a std::map and an order-ID hash map') that must be parsed twice. The ending tacks two results onto one 'which' clause ('ran the full replay at ... and hit a 1.2 µs p99 on a separate 2M-event run'), breaking the one-sentence 'did X to accomplish Y, which did Z' rule. 'p99' of what (per-event processing, per-order, wall clock including parsing?) is not stated, and the 1.2 µs is from a different run than the 1.26M events/sec, so the two numbers can't be read together. Also, an HFT interviewer will see std::list + std::map (node-based, cache-unfriendly) and immediately ask why; the bullet presents this as a design win without showing awareness of that tradeoff.
feedback.why_it_matters: This is the bullet a trading-systems interviewer will probe hardest. An unlabeled p99 from a separate run looks like cherry-picking, and the container choice invites a 'why not a flat array / intrusive list?' question the page doesn't prepare for.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the 1.2 µs p99 measures (per-event latency of which operation) and why it comes from a separate 2M-event run rather than the full replay
feedback.suggested_direction: Say the structure in plain words before the type names (a FIFO queue at each price, plus a lookup from order ID to its spot in the queue), keep one result in the 'which' clause, and label the p99. Move or drop the second metric rather than stitching it on with 'and'.

feedback.bullet: Designed the order book with std::list FIFOs per price level in a std::map and an order-ID hash map to make cancels O(1), which ran the full replay at 1.26M events/sec and hit a 1.2 µs p99 on a separate 2M-event run
feedback.problem: The p99 does not say what it is the 99th percentile of (per-message processing in the book? per add/cancel/execute? including parsing?), and the bullet switches units from 'messages' (bullet 1: 50.9M messages) to 'events' (here: 1.26M events/sec) without saying whether they are the same thing. It also does not say whether these numbers were taken before or after the core-pinning fix described in bullet 4.
feedback.why_it_matters: A low-latency reader's first question is 'p99 of what, measured where, on which setup'. 1.26M/sec implies a ~0.8 µs mean per event, so a 1.2 µs p99 is plausible only if both cover the same unit of work; if the reader can't confirm that, the two numbers look like they came from different benchmarks stitched together.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what operation the 1.2 µs p99 times (and whether it includes feed parsing); whether 'events' = the IEX messages from bullet 1; whether the runs were core-pinned
feedback.suggested_direction: Name the timed operation next to the percentile and use one noun (messages or events) across bullets 1-2, e.g. '...1.2 µs p99 per-message book update on a separate 2M-message run'. If the runs were pinned, a two-word 'pinned core' tag removes the ambiguity with bullet 4.

feedback.problem: This is the longest bullet in Experience and stacks two tool names (AnyGrasp, Open3D) between the setup and the purpose. It also has nothing to do with the low-latency target.
feedback.why_it_matters: It takes up two full lines in a section the HFT reader will skim past. That's minor, but it competes with the stronger systems evidence.
feedback.suggested_direction: Trim to the purpose and method (draw candidate grasps on images so the VLM avoids collisions), and move 'Open3D' to Skills if it's needed.

feedback.bullet: Built and prompt-tuned a pipeline for a PhD-led robotics project aimed at ICLR that overlays AnyGrasp’s candidate grasps on camera images in Open3D to help a vision-language model pick grasps that avoid hitting the table
feedback.problem: Four nested qualifiers ('for a PhD-led robotics project aimed at ICLR that overlays ... in Open3D to help ...') make the sentence a chain rather than one clean 'did X to accomplish Y, which did Z'. There is no 'which did Z' outcome at all. 'aimed at ICLR' signals an unaccepted submission and the candidate's contribution vs. the PhD student's is ambiguous. 'in Open3D' is a tool mention that doesn't explain the engineering.
feedback.why_it_matters: For an HFT reader this is the least relevant bullet on the page and also the hardest to parse, so it costs attention without adding signal; the ICLR mention invites 'what's your name on?' questions.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: which part of the pipeline the candidate owned, and whether there is any observed outcome (e.g. fewer table collisions)
feedback.suggested_direction: Cut 'PhD-led' / 'aimed at ICLR' or move them out of the sentence's critical path, drop 'in Open3D', and end on what the overlay accomplished. Shortening is the main lever.

feedback.bullet: Built and prompt-tuned a pipeline for a PhD-led robotics project aimed at ICLR that overlays AnyGrasp’s candidate grasps on camera images in Open3D to help a vision-language model pick grasps that avoid hitting the table
feedback.problem: No outcome, and the content (prompt-tuning, VLM grasp selection) is unrelated to low-latency systems; it takes two lines of a page whose strength is the C++ project.
feedback.why_it_matters: For a trading-systems screen this bullet adds breadth but no hiring signal; it is low cost but dilutes the systems story.
feedback.suggested_direction: Acceptable to keep; if space is needed for clarifications in the project bullets, this is the first candidate to shorten to one line.

bullet_groups.bullet: Traced an apparent 1.65x regression to the CPU frequency governor with perf counters and a do-nothing control book to rule out a code change, which led to core pinning that cut run-to-run variance from 6% to 0.06%

feedback.bullet: Traced an apparent 1.65x regression to the CPU frequency governor with perf counters and a do-nothing control book to rule out a code change, which led to core pinning that cut run-to-run variance from 6% to 0.06%
feedback.problem: 'do-nothing control book' is a coined phrase that a non-engineer, and maybe some engineers, will stumble on. The 'which led to' chain makes it one long breath.
feedback.why_it_matters: This is a strong debugging story for HFT. The odd phrase is the only spot where a reader has to re-read it.
feedback.suggested_direction: Rephrase 'do-nothing control book' as a plain description, e.g. 'a baseline build that did no matching work', keeping the rest as is.

feedback.bullet: Traced an apparent 1.65x regression to the CPU frequency governor with perf counters and a do-nothing control book to rule out a code change, which led to core pinning that cut run-to-run variance from 6% to 0.06%
feedback.problem: Slight mechanism gap: the cause is the frequency governor, but the fix named is core pinning, which addresses migration rather than frequency scaling. Also long for two lines.
feedback.why_it_matters: An interviewer who knows perf tuning will ask why pinning fixed a governor problem; the answer should be on the page or ready.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whether the governor was also set (e.g. to performance) alongside pinning
feedback.suggested_direction: Make the fix match the diagnosis in wording, or be ready to explain the link; otherwise leave this bullet alone, it is the most interview-ready one on the page.

feedback.bullet: Traced an apparent 1.65x regression to the CPU frequency governor with perf counters and a do-nothing control book to rule out a code change, which led to core pinning that cut run-to-run variance from 6% to 0.06%
feedback.problem: 'run-to-run variance from 6% to 0.06%' does not say which metric varied (throughput? p99?), how it is computed (coefficient of variation? max-min spread?), or over how many runs. The cause is the frequency governor but the fix named is core pinning; a reader expects the governor to be fixed (performance mode / fixed frequency) and wonders whether pinning alone explains a 100x drop.
feedback.why_it_matters: A 100x variance reduction is the most striking number on the page and the easiest to challenge; without the metric and run count it reads as a possibly lucky small sample. The cause/fix mismatch makes the diagnosis look less rigorous than the control-book method suggests.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: which measurement's variance, how computed, number of runs; whether the governor was also set as part of the fix
feedback.suggested_direction: Name the measured quantity and run count in place of the bare word 'variance' (e.g. 'cut throughput spread across N runs from 6% to 0.06%'), and make the fix match the cause ('...led to pinning cores and [the governor change, if one was made]').

bullet_groups.bullet: Precomputed popular workflows from a 270K+ row PostgreSQL table into a Redis-cached category tree to keep lookups within the database's permission and rate limits, which became the Claude skill's main search tool

feedback.bullet: Precomputed popular workflows from a 270K+ row PostgreSQL table into a Redis-cached category tree to keep lookups within the database's permission and rate limits, which became the Claude skill's main search tool
feedback.problem: Three unexplained ideas are packed into one sentence: 'category tree', 'permission and rate limits', and 'the Claude skill'. I can't tell what problem the limits caused (was the tool blocked, slow, or not allowed to query directly?) or who benefited.
feedback.why_it_matters: I can't pass this to a hiring manager without guessing, so the second Capital One bullet adds nothing to my screen beyond the word 'Redis'.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what went wrong when the AI tool queried the database directly (blocked by permissions, throttled, too slow), stated before the fix
feedback.suggested_direction: Lead with the constraint in plain words, then the fix, then that it became the main search tool; drop either 'PostgreSQL' or 'Redis-cached' from the sentence if the Skills line already carries it.

feedback.bullet: Precomputed popular workflows from a 270K+ row PostgreSQL table into a Redis-cached category tree to keep lookups within the database’s permission and rate limits, which became the Claude skill’s main search tool
feedback.problem: 'Redis-cached category tree' is a noun stack, and 'Precomputed popular workflows ... into a ... category tree' doesn't say what was precomputed (rankings? groupings? the workflows themselves?). The mechanism for 'within the database's permission ... limits' is unclear: caching explains rate limits, but not how it resolves a permissions constraint. 'which became the Claude skill's main search tool' is an adoption claim with unclear ownership (did the candidate wire it in, or did the team choose it?).
feedback.why_it_matters: A reader can't restate this bullet, and 'permission limits' solved by a cache sounds like either a misunderstanding or a workaround of access controls, which is a bad look at a bank.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what 'popular workflows' were precomputed into, and what the permission limit was (e.g. the skill couldn't query the table directly)
feedback.suggested_direction: Lead with the constraint in plain words (the skill couldn't query the table directly / often enough), then say what was cached and how it was organized. Replace 'Redis-cached category tree' with a verb phrase such as 'grouped them by category and cached them in Redis'.

bullet_groups.bullet: Implemented B+ tree and LSM-tree backends for the engine’s event log to compare them on identical 2M-record workloads, which showed the B+ tree giving 12.8x the read throughput and 22x faster range queries for 27% more disk

feedback.bullet: Implemented B+ tree and LSM-tree backends for the engine’s event log to compare them on identical 2M-record workloads, which showed the B+ tree giving 12.8x the read throughput and 22x faster range queries for 27% more disk
feedback.problem: Mechanism is unclear: an event log is normally append-only, so the reader doesn't know why a matching engine's log needs indexed reads or range queries at all, or what was being looked up. LSM trees are write-optimized, yet only read results are reported, which looks like the comparison was framed to favor the B+ tree. 'for 27% more disk' is a telegraphic fragment (dropped 'at the cost of'). Three metrics stacked in one clause.
feedback.why_it_matters: A systems interviewer's first question will be 'what about write throughput?' and 'why does an event log need range queries?'. Without that, the bullet reads like a textbook exercise bolted onto the project rather than a decision driven by the engine.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what queries the event log has to serve, and how the two backends compared on writes (if measured)
feedback.suggested_direction: State the read pattern that motivated the comparison before naming the trees, and spell out the tradeoff in words ('at the cost of 27% more disk'). Consider dropping one of the three numbers.

feedback.bullet: Implemented B+ tree and LSM-tree backends for the engine’s event log to compare them on identical 2M-record workloads, which showed the B+ tree giving 12.8x the read throughput and 22x faster range queries for 27% more disk
feedback.problem: Only the read-side results are reported; write/ingest throughput, which is the LSM tree's main reason to exist and the dominant operation for an append-heavy event log, is absent, and the workload mix ('identical 2M-record workloads') is not described.
feedback.why_it_matters: A storage-literate reader sees a comparison that reports only the dimensions where the B+ tree wins and suspects cherry-picking or a read-heavy workload that was never stated. It also invites 'why would you put an event log in a B+ tree?', which the bullet doesn't answer.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: read/write mix of the workload; whether write throughput was measured and how the two compared
feedback.suggested_direction: State the workload shape in a few words before the result (e.g. 'on identical read-heavy 2M-record workloads') or, if write numbers exist, give the trade-off in both directions instead of '27% more disk' alone.
